extracted.intended_audience: artists, writers, critics, and general readers interested in standards for what constitutes good art
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging/producing art focused on intelligibility, universality, moral/sincere feeling, and avoidance of artificial obscurity across poetry, painting, music, drama, and prose. Emphasises accessibility to broad audiences and rejection of obscurity-as-merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to obscurity as a merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Haziness, mysteriousness, obscurity, and exclusiveness (shutting out the masses) should not be elevated to the rank of a merit or a condition of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy identifies Symbolist/Decadent poets (Baudelaire, Verlaine, Mallarmé) and others who deliberately cultivate obscurity—pieces whose meanings 'have to be guessed like a rebus'—as anti-examples. Deliberate allusiveness, puzzles, and making 'enigme' the aim of poetry are criticized as destructive to art's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and intelligibility to the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Art must be intelligible and communicative to a wide audience; its language should be understood by all and 'infect' any man whatever his plane of development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy argues that great art (e.g., Gospel parables, folk-legends, epics) is accessible to ordinary people; art differs from technical knowledge and should not require specialised preparation. If a supposed masterpiece cannot be understood by the masses, that is evidence it may be bad art or not art at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness, definiteness, and eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should avoid incorrectness, indefiniteness, and lack of eloquence; precision and well-chosen expression are virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy points to faulty comparisons and unclear imagery (e.g., Mallarmé, Verlaine examples where 'how can snow shine like sand?') as signs of poor artistry. Maintain definite, correct use of language and imagery rather than vague or incorrect analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity, naiveté, and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine feeling—naïveté, sincerity, and simplicity—are essential qualities of good art; art should not be dominated by affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy criticises Baudelaire and Verlaine for lacking these qualities and for showing more of the author than of the subject. Good art transmits feeling honestly rather than showcasing the artist's cleverness or pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificiality and forced originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should not be artificially novel or forced in pursuit of originality; contrived forms and 'forced originality' are defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When novelty is sought chiefly to refresh amusement of an elite class (changing form while keeping the same shallow substance), critics and publics may hail it, but Tolstoy regards such novelty—often accompanied by pornographic or eccentric detail—as decline, not true innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality and moral/religious rootedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The best art conveys universal feelings (often religious or moral) that are common to humanity and therefore comprehensible across cultures and classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy uses examples like Genesis, Gospel parables, folk-songs, and the hymns of the Vedas to show art that transmits elevated feelings to all. Art founded on man's relation to God or shared moral perception will be widely accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's purpose is to transmit feeling, not intellectual argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Art's business is to make understood and felt what might otherwise require argument; it acts through emotional transmission rather than logical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish art from disciplines requiring sequential technical knowledge (e.g., mathematics). A work of art should evoke recognition and feeling in the recipient rather than demand preparatory study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability over mere habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work is claimed to be 'very good but difficult', there should be an explanatory knowledge that makes it understandable; insisting that repeated exposure (habituation) will make it comprehensible is not a satisfactory justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy says telling people to 'read and hear again and again' is only habituation, analogous to becoming accustomed to bad food or drink; explanation and teaching are needed if difficulty is genuine, otherwise the work may simply be bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility across social classes; reject exclusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should not be exclusive to the upper classes or 'the elect'; separating art from universal audiences leads to decline in art's value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy warns that when art becomes the pastime of a narrow class and seeks novelty to amuse itself, it becomes ever more incomprehensible and understood only by a shrinking circle—ultimately defeating art's social function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of narrative, subject, and form across media
rubrics_metrics.description: Across novels, drama, painting, and music, works should make their subject, actions, and agents comprehensible (e.g., in storytelling: who, what, where?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy highlights modern novels, plays, and musical pieces that are 'abscons'—where one cannot tell what is happening, to whom, or why—as failures. Ensure that form and subject are clear enough for the audience to grasp the intended impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pornographic detail and glorified egotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should not elevate gross egotism or parade pornographic details as a stylistic merit; moral degradation of subject-matter undermines art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy cites Baudelaire's preference for painted faces and artificiality and the use of pornographic detail to 'freshen' art as an indicator of decadence rather than value. Ethical content matters to artistic worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should not be mere novelty to freshen amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventing new forms solely to vary the amusements of a social class (changing form while keeping identical shallow substance) is not genuine artistic progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy compares this to changing card-games to relieve tedium; substituting form for substantive moral or emotional content results in an art of fashion and novelty, not of enduring value.
